q002.question: Como desativar os logs de exceção do OpenTelemetry no FastAPI?
q002.answer:
Para desativar os logs de exceção do OpenTelemetry no FastAPI, você pode definir a propriedade `logs` para `False` em seu código.

Fontes: [1]

sources.text:
### Inspect errors

FastAPI records unhandled exceptions as OpenTelemetry logs, linked to the request's or connection's trace. Error logs are recorded even when the trace is not sampled.

Exception logs include the exception's type, message, and stack trace. Messages and stack traces can contain sensitive information. Use your provider's log processors to filter or redact them, or set `logs` to `False` to disable these logs.

FastAPI also records request validation failures as warning logs with the route and error count. These logs do not include the invalid input.

q004.question: Como o FastAPI distingue parâmetros de caminho de parâmetros de consulta?
q004.answer: O FastAPI distingue parâmetros de caminho de parâmetros de consulta através do nome dos parâmetros declarados. Você pode declarar tanto parâmetros de caminho quanto parâmetros de consulta simultaneamente, e o FastAPI sabe distinguir entre eles devido ao nome dos parâmetros. Por exemplo, em um endpoint como `/users/{user_id}/items/{item_id}`, `user_id` é um parâmetro de caminho e `item_id` é um parâmetro de consulta. Fontes: [1]
q004.translated: How does FastAPI distinguish between path parameters and query parameters?
q004.raw:
O FastAPI distingue parâmetros de caminho de parâmetros de consulta usando o nome dos parâmetros declarados. Neste exemplo, você pode ver que os parâmetros `user_id` e `item_id`, que fazem parte da URL, são considerados parâmetros de caminho. Já `q` e `short` são considerados parâmetros de consulta, pois são declarados após a barra `/` e antes dos parâmetros de caminho.

q005.question: Como sobrescrever uma dependência em testes?
q005.answer:
Para sobrescrever uma dependência em testes, você pode usar o atributo `app.dependency_overrides` de seu aplicativo FastAPI. Você define uma nova função como valor para a chave que é a dependência original que deseja substituir. Isso permite que você forneça uma nova dependência que será usada apenas durante os testes.

Fontes: [1] [3]

sources.text:
# Testing Dependencies with Overrides

## Overriding dependencies during testing

There are some scenarios where you might want to override a dependency during testing.

You don't want the original dependency to run (nor any of the sub-dependencies it might have).

Instead, you want to provide a different dependency that will be used only during tests (possibly only some specific tests), and will provide a value that can be used where the value of the original dependency was used.

### Use the `app.dependency_overrides` attribute

For these cases, your **FastAPI** application has an attribute `app.dependency_overrides`, it is a simple `dict`.

To override a dependency for testing, you put as a key the original dependency (a function), and as the value, your dependency override (another function).

And then **FastAPI** will call that override instead of the original dependency.

q005.translated: How do you override a dependency in tests?
q005.raw:
Para sobrescrever uma dependência em testes no FastAPI, você pode usar o atributo `app.dependency_overrides`. Você define uma nova função como valor para a chave original dependência que deseja sobrescrever. Isso permite que você forneça um valor diferente durante os testes, que será usado em vez da dependência original.

q007.question: O que se pode definir sobre webhooks usando OpenAPI no FastAPI?
q007.answer:
O FastAPI permite definir o nome dos webhooks, os tipos de operações HTTP que o aplicativo pode enviar (como POST, PUT, etc.) e os corpos de solicitação que o aplicativo enviará usando OpenAPI.

Fontes: [1]

sources.text:
## Documenting webhooks with **FastAPI** and OpenAPI

With **FastAPI**, using OpenAPI, you can define the names of these webhooks, the types of HTTP operations that your app can send (e.g. `POST`, `PUT`, etc.) and the request **bodies** that your app would send.

This can make it a lot easier for your users to **implement their APIs** to receive your **webhook** requests, they might even be able to autogenerate some of their own API code.

**Note**

Webhooks are available in OpenAPI 3.1.0 and above, supported by FastAPI `0.99.0` and above.

q010.question: Por que o código de saída de uma dependência precisa rodar antes das subdependências?
q010.answer:
O código de saída de uma dependência precisa rodar antes das subdependências para garantir que a dependência ainda possa usar as subdependências durante seu próprio código de saída. Isso é importante porque a dependência pode precisar de acesso a valores ou estado gerenciados pelas subdependências durante a execução de seu próprio código de saída.

Fontes: [1]

sources.text:
### `scope` for sub-dependencies

When you declare a dependency with a `scope="request"` (the default), any sub-dependency needs to also have a `scope` of `"request"`.

But a dependency with `scope` of `"function"` can have dependencies with `scope` of `"function"` and `scope` of `"request"`.

This is because any dependency needs to be able to run its exit code before the sub-dependencies, as it might need to still use them during its exit code.

q010.translated: Why does the output code of a dependency need to run before its subdependencies?
q010.raw:
O código de saída de uma dependência precisa rodar antes das subdependências para garantir que a dependência ainda possa usar as subdependências durante seu próprio código de saída. Isso é importante porque a dependência pode precisar de acesso a subdependências durante o seu próprio código de saída, mesmo que isso ocorra após o retorno da função de operação de caminho.

q012.question: Para que tipos de dados o streaming de JSON Lines pode ser usado?
q012.answer:
Streaming de JSON Lines pode ser usado para enviar sequências de dados estruturados como JSON. É especialmente útil quando você precisa enviar dados em uma sequência, como uma série de objetos JSON separados por linhas, sem esperar que todos os dados estejam prontos antes de começar a enviar.

Fontes: [3] [4]

sources.text:
# Stream Data

If you want to stream data that can be structured as JSON, you should [Stream JSON Lines](../tutorial/stream-json-lines.md).

But if you want to **stream pure binary data** or strings, here's how you can do it.

**Note**

Added in FastAPI 0.134.0.

# Stream JSON Lines

You could have a sequence of data that you would like to send in a "**stream**", you could do it with **JSON Lines**.

**Note**

Added in FastAPI 0.134.0.

## What is a Stream?

"**Streaming**" data means that your app will start sending data items to the client without waiting for the entire sequence of items to be ready.

So, it will send the first item, the client will receive and start processing it, and you might still be producing the next item.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant Client

    App->>App: Produce Item 1
    App->>Client: Send Item 1
    App->>App: Produce Item 2
    Client->>Client: Process Item 1
    App->>Client: Send Item 2
    App->>App: Produce Item 3
    Client->>Client: Process Item 2
    App->>Client: Send Item 3
    Client->>Client: Process Item 3
    Note over App: Keeps producing...
    Note over Client: Keeps consuming...
```

It could even be an infinite stream, where you keep sending data.

q012.translated: For which data types is JSON Lines streaming used?
q012.raw:
Streaming de JSON Lines pode ser usado para enviar sequências de dados estruturados como JSON. É especialmente útil quando você precisa enviar dados em uma sequência, como uma série de objetos JSON semelhante a um array JSON, mas separados por linhas em vez de colchetes e vírgulas.

q015.question: O que o sistema de Injeção de Dependências faz com a árvore hierárquica de dependências?
q015.answer:
O sistema de Injeção de Dependências cria e organiza uma árvore hierárquica de dependências, onde cada função ou objeto dependente pode ter dependências próprias. O sistema FastAPI cuida de resolver todas essas dependências e fornecer (injetar) os resultados em cada etapa, garantindo que a árvore hierárquica de dependências seja construída de forma eficiente e eficaz.

Fontes: [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]

sources.text:
## Simple and Powerful

Although the hierarchical dependency injection system is very simple to define and use, it's still very powerful.

You can define dependencies that in turn can define dependencies themselves.

In the end, a hierarchical tree of dependencies is built, and the **Dependency Injection** system takes care of solving all these dependencies for you (and their sub-dependencies) and providing (injecting) the results at each step.

For example, let's say you have 4 API endpoints (*path operations*):

* `/items/public/`
* `/items/private/`
* `/users/{user_id}/activate`
* `/items/pro/`

then you could add different permission requirements for each of them just with dependencies and sub-dependencies:

## What is "Dependency Injection"

**"Dependency Injection"** means, in programming, that there is a way for your code (in this case, your *path operation functions*) to declare things that it requires to work and use: "dependencies".

And then, that system (in this case **FastAPI**) will take care of doing whatever is needed to provide your code with those needed dependencies ("inject" the dependencies).

This is very useful when you need to:

* Have shared logic (the same code logic again and again).
* Share database connections.
* Enforce security, authentication, role requirements, etc.
* And many other things...

All these, while minimizing code repetition.

## Dependency Injection

Using `BackgroundTasks` also works with the dependency injection system, you can declare a parameter of type `BackgroundTasks` at multiple levels: in a *path operation function*, in a dependency (dependable), in a sub-dependency, etc.

**FastAPI** knows what to do in each case and how to reuse the same object, so that all the background tasks are merged together and are run in the background afterwards:

### Dependency Injection

FastAPI includes an extremely easy to use, but extremely powerful <dfn title='also known as "components", "resources", "services", "providers"'>**Dependency Injection**</dfn> system.

* Even dependencies can have dependencies, creating a hierarchy or **"graph" of dependencies**.
* All **automatically handled** by the framework.
* All the dependencies can require data from requests and **augment the path operation** constraints and automatic documentation.
* **Automatic validation** even for *path operation* parameters defined in dependencies.
* Support for complex user authentication systems, **database connections**, etc.
* **No compromise** with databases, frontends, etc. But easy integration with all of them.

## Recap

Apart from all the fancy words used here, the **Dependency Injection** system is quite simple.

Just functions that look the same as the *path operation functions*.

But still, it is very powerful, and allows you to declare arbitrarily deeply nested dependency "graphs" (trees).

**Tip**

All this might not seem as useful with these simple examples.

But you will see how useful it is in the chapters about **security**.

And you will also see the amounts of code it will save you.

q017.question: Qual a diferença entre a `HTTPException` do FastAPI e a do Starlette?
q017.answer:
A principal diferença entre a `HTTPException` do FastAPI e a do Starlette é que o FastAPI permite que qualquer dado JSON-able seja usado como detalhe (`detail`) da exceção, enquanto o Starlette só aceita strings para esse campo.

Fontes: [1]

sources.text:
#### FastAPI's `HTTPException` vs Starlette's `HTTPException`

**FastAPI** has its own `HTTPException`.

And **FastAPI**'s `HTTPException` error class inherits from Starlette's `HTTPException` error class.

The only difference is that **FastAPI**'s `HTTPException` accepts any JSON-able data for the `detail` field, while Starlette's `HTTPException` only accepts strings for it.

So, you can keep raising **FastAPI**'s `HTTPException` as normally in your code.

But when you register an exception handler, you should register it for Starlette's `HTTPException`.

This way, if any part of Starlette's internal code, or a Starlette extension or plug-in, raises a Starlette `HTTPException`, your handler will be able to catch and handle it.

In this example, to be able to have both `HTTPException`s in the same code, Starlette's exceptions is renamed to `StarletteHTTPException`:

```Python
from starlette.exceptions import HTTPException as StarletteHTTPException
```

q019.question: Qual a vantagem de guardar as senhas com hash caso o banco de dados seja roubado?
q019.answer: Guardar as senhas com hash, mesmo que o banco de dados seja roubado, garante que os ladrões não possam usar essas senhas em outros sistemas. Isso é porque os ladrões só terão os hashes das senhas, e não as senhas em formato de texto plano. Portanto, eles não poderão tentar usar essas mesmas senhas em outros sistemas, o que seria perigoso porque muitas pessoas usam a mesma senha em vários lugares. Fontes: [1] [2] [3]

sources.text:
# Extra Models

Continuing with the previous example, it will be common to have more than one related model.

This is especially the case for user models, because:

* The **input model** needs to be able to have a password.
* The **output model** should not have a password.
* The **database model** would probably need to have a hashed password.

**Danger**

Never store user's plaintext passwords. Always store a "secure hash" that you can then verify.

If you don't know, you will learn what a "password hash" is in the [security chapters](security/simple-oauth2.md#password-hashing).

##### Why use password hashing

If your database is stolen, the thief won't have your users' plaintext passwords, only the hashes.

So, the thief won't be able to try to use those same passwords in another system (as many users use the same password everywhere, this would be dangerous).

### Why use password hashing

If your database is stolen, the thief won't have your users' plaintext passwords, only the hashes.

So, the thief won't be able to try to use that password in another system (as many users use the same password everywhere, this would be dangerous).

Isso impede que o ladrão use essas mesmas senhas em outro sistema (pois muitos usuários usam a mesma senha em vários lugares, o que seria perigoso).

In this example above, the input model is a Pydantic v1 model, and the output model (defined in `response_model=ItemV2`) is a Pydantic v2 model.

### Pydantic v1 parameters

If you need to use some of the FastAPI-specific tools for parameters like `Body`, `Query`, `Form`, etc. with Pydantic v1 models, you can import them from `fastapi.temp_pydantic_v1_params` while you finish the migration to Pydantic v2:

```python
from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.temp_pydantic_v1_params import Body
from pydantic.v1 import BaseModel

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str | None = None
    size: float

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/items/")
async def create_item(item: Annotated[Item, Body(embed=True)]) -> Item:
    return item
```

q022.question: Por que combinar respostas predefinidas com respostas específicas de cada operação de rota?
q022.answer:
Por que combinar respostas predefinidas com respostas específicas de cada operação de rota?

Combinar respostas predefinidas com respostas específicas de cada operação de rota permite que você reutilize as respostas padrão para cenários comuns, enquanto ainda oferece a flexibilidade de personalizar as respostas para casos mais específicos. Isso é útil para evitar duplicar código e manter a consistência na documentação.

Fontes: [1] [3] [4]

sources.text:
## Combine predefined responses and custom ones

You might want to have some predefined responses that apply to many *path operations*, but you want to combine them with custom responses needed by each *path operation*.

For those cases, you can use the Python technique of "unpacking" a `dict` with `**dict_to_unpack`:

```Python
old_dict = {
    "old key": "old value",
    "second old key": "second old value",
}
new_dict = {**old_dict, "new key": "new value"}
```

Here, `new_dict` will contain all the key-value pairs from `old_dict` plus the new key-value pair:

```Python
{
    "old key": "old value",
    "second old key": "second old value",
    "new key": "new value",
}
```

You can use that technique to reuse some predefined responses in your *path operations* and combine them with additional custom ones.

For example:

* They will be marked with a list of tags that contain a single string `"items"`.
    * These "tags" are especially useful for the automatic interactive documentation systems (using OpenAPI).
* All of them will include the predefined `responses`.
* All these *path operations* will have the list of `dependencies` evaluated/executed before them.
    * If you also declare dependencies in a specific *path operation*, **they will be executed too**.
    * The router dependencies are executed first, then the [`dependencies` in the decorator](dependencies/dependencies-in-path-operation-decorators.md), and then the normal parameter dependencies.
    * You can also add [`Security` dependencies with `scopes`](../advanced/security/oauth2-scopes.md).

**Tip**

Having `dependencies` in the `APIRouter` can be used, for example, to require authentication for a whole group of *path operations*. Even if the dependencies are not added individually to each one of them.

**Tip**

## Combining information

You can also combine response information from multiple places, including the `response_model`, `status_code`, and `responses` parameters.

You can declare a `response_model`, using the default status code `200` (or a custom one if you need), and then declare additional information for that same response in `responses`, directly in the OpenAPI schema.

**FastAPI** will keep the additional information from `responses`, and combine it with the JSON Schema from your model.

For example, you can declare a response with a status code `404` that uses a Pydantic model and has a custom `description`.

q024.question: Por que não dá para declarar campos `Body` em JSON junto com parâmetros `File` e `Form`?
q024.answer:
Por que não dá para declarar campos `Body` em JSON junto com parâmetros `File` e `Form`? Isso não é permitido por causa da natureza do protocolo HTTP. O FastAPI segue as regras do protocolo HTTP, que determina que os campos `File` e `Form` são enviados como `multipart/form-data`, enquanto os campos `Body` em JSON são enviados como `application/json`.

Fontes: [1] [2]

sources.text:
You can declare multiple `File` and `Form` parameters in a *path operation*, but you can't also declare `Body` fields that you expect to receive as JSON, as the request will have the body encoded using `multipart/form-data` instead of `application/json`.

This is not a limitation of **FastAPI**, it's part of the HTTP protocol.

## Define `File` and `Form` parameters

Create file and form parameters the same way you would for `Body` or `Query`:

```python
from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import FastAPI, File, Form, UploadFile

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/files/")
async def create_file(
    file: Annotated[bytes, File()],
    fileb: Annotated[UploadFile, File()],
    token: Annotated[str, Form()],
):
    return {
        "file_size": len(file),
        "token": token,
        "fileb_content_type": fileb.content_type,
    }
```

The files and form fields will be uploaded as form data and you will receive the files and form fields.

And you can declare some of the files as `bytes` and some as `UploadFile`.

**Warning**

You can declare multiple `File` and `Form` parameters in a *path operation*, but you can't also declare `Body` fields that you expect to receive as JSON, as the request will have the body encoded using `multipart/form-data` instead of `application/json`.

Essa é uma característica do protocolo HTTP e não da biblioteca **FastAPI**. Fontes:1 2

q029.question: Que status HTTP as utilidades de segurança retornavam, antes do FastAPI 0.122.0, após uma falha de autenticação?
q029.answer:
Resposta:

Antes do FastAPI 0.122.0, as utilidades de segurança retornavam o status HTTP `403 Forbidden` após uma falha de autenticação.

Fontes: [1]

sources.text:
# Use Old 403 Authentication Error Status Codes

Before FastAPI version `0.122.0`, when the integrated security utilities returned an error to the client after a failed authentication, they used the HTTP status code `403 Forbidden`.

Starting with FastAPI version `0.122.0`, they use the more appropriate HTTP status code `401 Unauthorized`, and return a sensible `WWW-Authenticate` header in the response, following the HTTP specifications, [RFC 7235](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7235#section-3.1), [RFC 9110](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110#name-401-unauthorized).

But if for some reason your clients depend on the old behavior, you can revert to it by overriding the method `make_not_authenticated_error` in your security classes.

q032.question: O que o desenvolvedor passa a controlar ao usar `StreamingResponse`?
q032.answer: O desenvolvedor passa a controlar a forma como os dados são produzidos e codificados exatamente como ele precisa ser enviado, independentemente das anotações de tipo. Fontes: [1] [4]

sources.text:
### `StreamingResponse`

Takes an async generator or a normal generator/iterator (a function with `yield`) and streams the response body.

```python
import anyio
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

app = FastAPI()

async def fake_video_streamer():
    for i in range(10):
        yield b"some fake video bytes"
        await anyio.sleep(0)

@app.get("/")
async def main():
    return StreamingResponse(fake_video_streamer())
```

**Note**: Technical Details

An `async` task can only be cancelled when it reaches an `await`. If there is no `await`, the generator (function with `yield`) can not be cancelled properly and may keep running even after cancellation is requested.

Since this small example does not need any `await` statements, we add an `await anyio.sleep(0)` to give the event loop a chance to handle cancellation.

This would be even more important with large or infinite streams.

**Tip**

This also means that with `StreamingResponse` you have the **freedom** and **responsibility** to produce and encode the data bytes exactly as you need them to be sent, independent of the type annotations. 🤓

q032.translated: What does the developer control when using `StreamingResponse`?
q032.raw:
Ao usar `StreamingResponse`, o desenvolvedor passa a controlar completamente a forma como os dados são produzidos e codificados para serem enviados. Ele tem a liberdade e responsabilidade de produzir e codificar os bytes de dados exatamente da maneira que deseja ser enviada, independentemente das anotações de tipo.

q034.answer: Benchmark costumam não refletir bem as ferramentas porque esses testes geralmente focam em desempenho básico, esquecendo de testar as funcionalidades adicionais que as ferramentas podem oferecer. Fontes: [1] [5]

sources.text:
## Benchmarks and speed

When you check the benchmarks, it is common to see several tools of different types compared as equivalent.

Specifically, to see Uvicorn, Starlette and FastAPI compared together (among many other tools).

The simpler the problem solved by the tool, the better performance it will get. And most of the benchmarks don't test the additional features provided by the tool.

The hierarchy is like:

* **Uvicorn**: an ASGI server
    * **Starlette**: (uses Uvicorn) a web microframework
        * **FastAPI**: (uses Starlette) an API microframework with several additional features for building APIs, with data validation, etc.

### [Sanic](https://sanic.readthedocs.io/en/latest/)

It was one of the first extremely fast Python frameworks based on `asyncio`. It was made to be very similar to Flask.

**Note**: Technical Details

It used [`uvloop`](https://github.com/MagicStack/uvloop) instead of the default Python `asyncio` loop. That's what made it so fast.

It clearly inspired Uvicorn and Starlette, that are currently faster than Sanic in open benchmarks.

**Tip**: Inspired **FastAPI** to

Find a way to have a crazy performance.

That's why **FastAPI** is based on Starlette, as it is the fastest framework available (tested by third-party benchmarks).

q037.question: O que vale ao adicionar dependências globais a toda a aplicação?
q037.answer:
Adicionar dependências globais a toda a aplicação permite que você crie dependências que serão aplicadas a todos os operadores de caminho da aplicação. Isso é útil para cenários onde você deseja que uma dependência seja usada em todas as partes da aplicação, não apenas em um determinado operador de caminho.

Fontes: [1] [3]

sources.text:
# Global Dependencies

For some types of applications you might want to add dependencies to the whole application.

Similar to the way you can [add `dependencies` to the *path operation decorators*](dependencies-in-path-operation-decorators.md), you can add them to the `FastAPI` application.

In that case, they will be applied to all the *path operations* in the application:

### Import `FastAPI`

You import and create a `FastAPI` class as normally.

And we can even declare [global dependencies](dependencies/global-dependencies.md) that will be combined with the dependencies for each `APIRouter`:

```python
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

from .dependencies import get_query_token, get_token_header
from .internal import admin
from .routers import items, users

app = FastAPI(dependencies=[Depends(get_query_token)])

app.include_router(users.router)
app.include_router(items.router)
app.include_router(
    admin.router,
    prefix="/admin",
    tags=["admin"],
    dependencies=[Depends(get_token_header)],
    responses={418: {"description": "I'm a teapot"}},
)

@app.get("/")
async def root():
    return {"message": "Hello Bigger Applications!"}
```

q037.raw:
Adicionar dependências globais a toda a aplicação do FastAPI permite que essas dependências sejam aplicadas a todos os operadores de caminho da aplicação. Isso é útil para cenários onde você deseja que certas funcionalidades ou dados sejam acessíveis em todas as partes da aplicação.

q040.question: Quem deve cuidar do HTTPS na frente da aplicação na maioria dos casos?
q040.answer:
Na maioria dos casos, é o proxy quem deve cuidar do HTTPS na frente da aplicação.

Fontes: [1] [2]

sources.text:
# Behind a Proxy

In many situations, you would use a **proxy** like Traefik or Nginx in front of your FastAPI app.

These proxies could handle HTTPS certificates and other things.

## Proxy Forwarded Headers

A **proxy** in front of your application would normally set some headers on the fly before sending the requests to your **server** to let the server know that the request was **forwarded** by the proxy, letting it know the original (public) URL, including the domain, that it is using HTTPS, etc.

The **server** started by `fastapi run` is capable of interpreting these headers, and then passing that information to your application.

But for security, as the server doesn't know it is behind a trusted proxy, it won't interpret those headers.

**Note**: Technical Details

The proxy headers are:

It is a common practice to have **one program/HTTP server** running on the server (the machine, host, etc.) and **managing all the HTTPS parts**: receiving the **encrypted HTTPS requests**, sending the **decrypted HTTP requests** to the actual HTTP application running in the same server (the **FastAPI** application, in this case), take the **HTTP response** from the application, **encrypt it** using the appropriate **HTTPS certificate** and sending it back to the client using **HTTPS**. This server is often called a **[TLS Termination Proxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TLS_termination_proxy)**.

Some of the options you could use as a TLS Termination Proxy are:

* Traefik (that can also handle certificate renewals)
* Caddy (that can also handle certificate renewals)
* Nginx
* HAProxy

q040.translated: Who should handle HTTPS in front of the application in most cases?
q040.raw:
Na maioria dos casos, é o programa/HTTP server que deve cuidar do HTTPS na frente da aplicação. Este programa recebe as requisições HTTPS criptografadas, envia as requisições HTTP não criptografadas para a aplicação real (que pode ser um FastAPI), e depois recebe a resposta da aplicação e a criptografa novamente usando o certificado HTTPS apropriado antes de enviar de volta ao cliente usando HTTPS. Este programa geralmente é chamado de **TLS Termination Proxy**.

Na maioria dos casos, é o proxy quem deve cuidar do HTTPS na frente da aplicação.
